explanations.answer: So they may live and take the land
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Moses says he's teaching them “…so that you may live and may enter and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you.” The teaching has a purpose, and it's a good one. Moses isn't just filling the air with words.

explanations.answer: So they may earn back their freedom
explanations.explanation: Freedom isn't the reason Moses gives here. He says the statutes and ordinances are so Israel may live and take possession of the land the LORD is giving them. Notice that it's a land being given, not a prize being earned. Moses keeps the reason simple, and so should we.

explanations.answer: So they may keep Moses as leader
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say a word about himself in that verse. His reason is that Israel may live and enter and take possession of the land the LORD is giving them. A little later he even says he won't be crossing the Jordan himself (Deuteronomy 4:22). So this sermon is about the people, not about him.

Not quite, friend. Moses says, “You must not add to or subtract from what I command you…” That means no adding and no trimming. I've been caught tossing extra chocolate chips into a batch nobody asked for, but Moses isn't talking about chips.

Right, friend. Moses says, “You must not add to or subtract from what I command you…” Nothing gets added and nothing gets cut. I've been known to toss extra chocolate chips into a batch, but God's commands aren't mine to adjust.

explanations.answer: Every one of them is alive today
explanations.explanation: That's what Moses says. “But you who held fast to the LORD your God are alive to this day, every one of you.” Every single one, with nobody missing. Notice what he sets side by side: those who followed Baal of Peor were destroyed, and those who held fast are alive.

explanations.answer: Most of them lost their homes
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that. He says, “But you who held fast to the LORD your God are alive to this day, every one of you.” Losing homes never comes up. The word that does come up is alive.

explanations.answer: They were sent back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't in this verse at all. Moses says those who held fast to the LORD “are alive to this day, every one of you.” Nobody gets sent anywhere. They're alive, and Moses is pointing right at them.

explanations.answer: This great nation is wise and understanding
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Moses says the peoples will hear of all these statutes and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” Wisdom is what shows. Even people who aren't part of Israel take notice.

explanations.answer: This great nation is rich and powerful
explanations.explanation: Money and muscle aren't what Moses says they'll notice. He says the peoples will say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” What gets noticed is how Israel keeps the statutes. That's wisdom, not wealth.

explanations.answer: This great nation is fierce and fearless
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that. The peoples hear of the statutes and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” Nothing about fierce, nothing about fearless. It's all about wisdom and understanding.
That's the word, friend. Moses asks what nation has a god “as near to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call on Him.” Whenever we call, He's near. Hold onto that one.
Close, but Moses says the opposite. The word is near: a god “as near to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call on Him.” When Israel calls, the LORD is near, not hidden.

Moses does call the statutes righteous in the very next verse (Deuteronomy 4:8). But the word in this blank is near. The LORD is “as near to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call on Him.”

explanations.answer: The things their eyes have seen
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's it. Moses says, “…so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen, and so that they do not slip from your heart as long as you live.” These are things Israel watched happen. A memory like that is worth guarding.
Moses doesn't mention ancestors' names in this warning. He says not to forget “the things your eyes have seen.” It's about what Israel saw for themselves, not a family tree.

explanations.answer: The promises they made to Moses
explanations.explanation: That's not in the verse, friend. Moses warns them not to forget “the things your eyes have seen,” so that these things don't slip from their hearts as long as they live. Nothing about promises to him.
That's right. Moses says, “Teach them to your children and grandchildren.” What Israel saw doesn't stop with them. It's meant to be passed down to the next generation, and the one after that.

Moses actually says the opposite. In the same breath as the warning, he says, “Teach them to your children and grandchildren.” What they saw isn't meant to stay with them. It's meant to be passed down.

explanations.answer: Blazing with fire up to the heavens
explanations.explanation: That's the mountain Moses describes. It was “a mountain blazing with fire to the heavens, with black clouds and deep darkness.” Imagine standing at the base of that. I think I'd have held onto my hat with my mustache.

explanations.answer: Wrapped in a soft white mist
explanations.explanation: Nothing soft about it, friend. Moses says the mountain was “blazing with fire to the heavens, with black clouds and deep darkness.” Fire and black clouds, not white mist.

explanations.answer: Quiet and green in the sunshine
explanations.explanation: I wish, but no. Moses says it was “a mountain blazing with fire to the heavens, with black clouds and deep darkness.” Fire, black clouds, deep darkness. Not the picnic kind of mountain.
Not this time, friend. Moses says, “You heard the sound of the words but saw no form; there was only a voice.” They heard. They didn't see a form. That detail matters a lot for what Moses says next.
That's right. Moses says, “You heard the sound of the words but saw no form; there was only a voice.” A voice, and no form to look at. Keep that in mind, because Moses leans on it.

Yes, friend. Moses says the LORD declared “His covenant, which He commanded you to follow—the Ten Commandments that He wrote on two tablets of stone.” Written in stone, and handed to the people. That's about as clear as it gets.
Close in sound, but no. The verse says, “the Ten Commandments that He wrote on two tablets of stone.” The LORD wrote His covenant on those tablets. Tribes aren't what He wrote.

That's a nice word, but it isn't the one here. Moses says the LORD declared His covenant, “the Ten Commandments that He wrote on two tablets of stone.” Commandments are what were written on the stone.

explanations.answer: An idol of any form or shape
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses says, “…do not act corruptly and make an idol for yourselves of any form or shape…” Israel saw no form at Horeb, so no form of any kind should be made into an idol. The phrase "any form" covers a lot of ground.

explanations.answer: An altar out of cut stones
explanations.explanation: Altars aren't what Moses is warning about in this verse. He says not to “make an idol for yourselves of any form or shape.” That's the warning, and he spells out the details in the verses right after.
Treaties don't come up here, friend. Moses warns them not to act corruptly and “make an idol for yourselves of any form or shape.” It's an idol he's talking about.

Moses doesn't give that loophole. He names a likeness of a male or female, any beast on the earth, any bird that flies, any creature that crawls, and any fish in the waters (Deuteronomy 4:16-18). Bird and fish are right there on the list. No shape gets a pass.

Right, friend. Moses lists a male or female, a beast on the earth, a bird that flies, a creature that crawls and a fish in the waters (Deuteronomy 4:16-18). Birds and fish are named on purpose. He's covering every corner.

Moses doesn't give that option. He says, “…do not be enticed to bow down and worship what the LORD your God has apportioned to all the nations under heaven.” There's no "as long as" attached. Bowing to them is what he warns against.

That's right. Moses says, “…do not be enticed to bow down and worship what the LORD your God has apportioned to all the nations under heaven.” No "as long as" is attached. The sun, moon and stars aren't to be bowed down to.
Yes, friend. Moses says the LORD brought them out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, “to be the people of His inheritance, as you are today.” Out of the furnace and into belonging. Not a bad trade.
Ruling isn't what the verse says. The LORD brought them out of Egypt “to be the people of His inheritance, as you are today.” That's the purpose Moses names.
Moses doesn't claim that. He says the LORD brought them out of the iron furnace “to be the people of His inheritance, as you are today.” They're the LORD's people, not Moses' servants.

That's right. Moses says he must die in this land, but then adds, “…But you shall cross over and take possession of that good land.” He's not crossing, but the people are. That's a hard thing to say out loud, and he says it plainly.

Moses says the opposite. He tells them he will not be crossing the Jordan, and then says, “…But you shall cross over and take possession of that good land.” His not crossing doesn't stop theirs. I think that was a heavy thing to say to them.

That's the word. Moses says, “For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.” He has just reminded them of the mountain blazing with fire, so I think it lands hard. Moses doesn't soften it.
Not quite, friend. The verse says, “For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.” Fire is the word Moses uses.
Not this one. Moses says, “For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.” The word is fire, not flood.
Moses says the opposite, friend. If they make an idol, he says, “You will not live long upon it, but will be utterly destroyed.” That's a heavy word. It's a warning meant to be taken seriously.
That's right. Moses says that if they act corruptly and make an idol, “You will not live long upon it, but will be utterly destroyed.” It's a heavy warning, and Moses states it plainly.
Yes. Moses says, “Then the LORD will scatter you among the peoples…” Scattered means spread out among other nations. That's the next thing he names, and it's a hard one.
Moab doesn't come up in this part. Moses says, “Then the LORD will scatter you among the peoples…” The word is scatter.
The wilderness isn't what Moses says here. He says, “Then the LORD will scatter you among the peoples…” They'd be spread among the peoples, not left where they are.

That's right. Moses says the LORD will scatter them among the peoples, “and only a few of you will survive among the nations to which the LORD will drive you.” It's a sobering line. I think this is one of the heavier parts of the sermon.

Moses actually says the opposite. The LORD will scatter them, “and only a few of you will survive among the nations to which the LORD will drive you.” Only a few, not most. It's a heavy part of the warning.

explanations.answer: With all their heart and soul
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Moses says, “But if from there you will seek the LORD your God, you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul.” Even from far away, the way back is open. All your heart, all your soul.

explanations.answer: With offerings of silver and gold
explanations.explanation: Silver and gold don't come up here. Moses says, “…you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul.” It's about how they seek, not what they bring.

explanations.answer: With a journey back to Horeb
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't mention a trip. He says they will find Him “if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul.” Even from among the nations, that's the way.

Yes, friend. Moses says, “For the LORD your God is a merciful God; He will not abandon you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers, which He swore to them by oath.” After all those warnings, this verse is a gift. Mercy gets the last word here.
Moses says the opposite. The LORD is “a merciful God; He will not abandon you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers…” Not distant. Merciful.
Not this one. The verse says, “For the LORD your God is a merciful God.” Moses has just said they heard His voice out of the fire, so silent doesn't fit anyway (Deuteronomy 4:12).

explanations.answer: Heard God's voice from the fire and lived
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses asks, “Has a people ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire, as you have, and lived?” Heard and lived. It's a question that expects one answer.

explanations.answer: Seen God's face on a mountain and lived
explanations.explanation: Seeing a face isn't what Moses says. He asks, “Has a people ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire, as you have, and lived?” They heard His voice. Earlier he reminded them they saw no form.

explanations.answer: Walked straight through a fire and lived
explanations.explanation: Walking through fire isn't what he asks about. Moses asks, “Has a people ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire, as you have, and lived?” It's hearing God's voice from the fire.

explanations.answer: So they'd know the LORD alone is God
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Moses says, “You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him.” That's the reason, plain and simple. Nothing added.

explanations.answer: So they'd know they were stronger than Egypt
explanations.explanation: That isn't the reason Moses gives. He says, “You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him.” The point isn't Israel's strength. It's who the LORD is.

explanations.answer: So they'd know Moses was a great leader
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't point to himself at all. He says, “You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him.” It's all about the LORD.

That's right. Moses says, “He let you hear His voice from heaven to discipline you…” He also showed them His great fire on earth, and they heard His words out of the fire. The reason given is discipline.
Moses doesn't say that. He says, “He let you hear His voice from heaven to discipline you…” The voice was for Israel, and the reason is discipline.
Reward isn't the word in the verse. Moses says, “He let you hear His voice from heaven to discipline you…” That's the reason the text gives, and I won't add one of my own.

That's what Moses says. “Because He loved your fathers, He chose their descendants after them and brought you out of Egypt by His presence and great power…” The reason is love, plain and simple. Not size, not a record.

explanations.answer: Because they were the largest nation
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that. The reason is, “Because He loved your fathers, He chose their descendants after them…” He even speaks of nations greater and mightier than them being driven out (Deuteronomy 4:38). Love is the reason, not size.

explanations.answer: Because they had kept every law
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason Moses gives. He says, “Because He loved your fathers, He chose their descendants after them…” The reason is love.

explanations.answer: So they and their children may prosper in the land
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Moses says, “Keep His statutes and commandments, which I am giving you today, so that you and your children after you may prosper, and that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time.” That's the sermon brought home. Your children are in it too.

explanations.answer: So they may win every battle without a fight
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't promise that. He says to keep the statutes and commandments “so that you and your children after you may prosper, and that you may live long in the land…” That's the reason he gives. Winning without a fight isn't in it.

explanations.answer: So Moses might cross the Jordan after all
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason. Moses has already said he will not be crossing the Jordan (Deuteronomy 4:22). He says to keep the statutes “so that you and your children after you may prosper, and that you may live long in the land.” It's for the people and their children.
